claim: Wild isolates of Saccharomyces cerevisiae tolerate chromosome amplification while laboratory strain W303 does not.
source: We previously showed that wild isolates of Saccharomyces cerevisiae tolerate chromosome amplification while laboratory strains used as a model for aneuploid syndromes do not.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The genetic basis for differential aneuploidy tolerance between wild and laboratory yeast strains maps to Ssd1.
source: Here, we mapped the genetic basis to Ssd1, an RNA-binding translational regulator that is functional in wild aneuploids but defective in laboratory strain W303.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic mapping experiments described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ssd1 is an RNA-binding translational regulator that is functional in wild aneuploids but defective in laboratory strain W303.
source: Here, we mapped the genetic basis to Ssd1, an RNA-binding translational regulator that is functional in wild aneuploids but defective in laboratory strain W303.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic mapping data and functional characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of SSD1 recapitulates myriad aneuploidy signatures previously taken as eukaryotic responses.
source: Loss of SSD1 recapitulates myriad aneuploidy signatures previously taken as eukaryotic responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic, proteomic, and phenotypic data presented in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: Aneuploidy tolerance is enabled via a role for Ssd1 in mitochondrial physiology, including binding and regulating nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs.
source: We show that aneuploidy tolerance is enabled via a role for Ssd1 in mitochondrial physiology, including binding and regulating nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs, coupled with a role in mitigating proteostasis stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data, proteomics, and functional assays shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Ssd1 has a role in mitigating proteostasis stress.
source: We show that aneuploidy tolerance is enabled via a role for Ssd1 in mitochondrial physiology, including binding and regulating nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs, coupled with a role in mitigating proteostasis stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by VHL-GFP and Hsp104-GFP aggregation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Recapitulating ssd1Δ defects with combinatorial drug treatment selectively blocked proliferation of wild-type aneuploids compared to euploids.
source: Recapitulating ssd1Δ defects with combinatorial drug treatment selectively blocked proliferation of wild-type aneuploids compared to euploids.
evidence: This claim is supported by drug treatment experiments with CCCP and NTC shown in Figure 6.

claim: Aneuploidy is highly detrimental during mammalian development.
source: Aneuploidy, in which cells carry an abnormal number of one or more chromosomes, is highly detrimental during mammalian development, since amplification of most human chromosomes is inviable during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about aneuploidy in mammalian development.

claim: Amplification of most human chromosomes is inviable during embryogenesis.
source: Aneuploidy, in which cells carry an abnormal number of one or more chromosomes, is highly detrimental during mammalian development, since amplification of most human chromosomes is inviable during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about human development.

claim: Imbalanced and elevated expression from altered chromosomes is thought to tax cellular proteostasis.
source: Imbalanced and especially elevated expression from altered chromosomes is thought to tax cellular proteostasis, both by producing too much protein and when stoichiometric imbalance of interacting proteins disrupts cooperative folding (Donnelly and Storchová, 2015; Oromendia and Amon, 2014; Pavelka and Rancati, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ≥90% of tumors are aneuploid with little detriment and even benefits to cells.
source: Yet ≥90% of tumors are aneuploid with little detriment and even benefits to cells, and the degree of aneuploidy is associated with poorer patient prognosis (Holland and Cleveland, 2012; Targa and Rancati, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The degree of aneuploidy is associated with poorer patient prognosis.

claim: Aneuploidy is common in several fungal species including fungal pathogens.
source: Aneuploidy is also common in several fungal species including fungal pathogens.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Chromosome amplification represents a major route to drug resistance in pathogenic infections.
source: In fact, chromosome amplification represents a major route to drug resistance in pathogenic infections, when amplification of drug transporters and defense mechanisms promotes drug evasion (Wertheimer et al., 2016; Ni et al., 2013; Bennett et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In laboratory strain W303, chromosome amplification leads to reduced cell growth.
source: In a well-studied laboratory strain, chromosome amplification leads to reduced cell growth, metabolic alterations, altered cell-cycle progression in part through aberrant cyclin regulation, activation of a common transcriptome program regardless of the amplified chromosome, and signatures of protein aggregation and defects clearing misfolded peptides, referred to as proteostasis stress (Torres et al., 2007; Torres et al., 2010; Oromendia et al., 2012; Sheltzer et al., 2012; Thorburn et al., 2013; Dephoure et al., 2014; Dodgson et al., 2016; Brennan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on W303 aneuploids.

claim: Chromosome amplification is beneficial in the right environment and provides a rapid route to phenotypic evolution.
source: Despite the deleterious effects reported in lab strains, chromosome amplification is beneficial in the right environment and provides a rapid route to phenotypic evolution (Rancati et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Yona et al., 2012; Filteau et al., 2015; Fontanillas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A substantial number of wild yeast strains are naturally aneuploid, in some cases carrying extra copies of multiple chromosomes.
source: However, we previously reported a striking difference among wild isolates: a substantial number of wild strains are naturally aneuploid, in some cases carrying extra copies of multiple chromosomes (Gasch et al., 2016; Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Over 20% of sequenced yeast strains are aneuploid, with each of the 16 yeast chromosomes represented across affected strains.
source: Recent large-scale sequencing efforts provide confirmatory evidence, reporting over 20% of sequenced strains as aneuploid, with each of the 16 yeast chromosomes represented across affected strains (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a large-scale sequencing study.

claim: Naturally aneuploid yeast show only subtle growth defects compared to laboratory strain W303.
source: In contrast to well-studied laboratory strain W303, naturally aneuploid yeast show only subtle growth defects, no detectable metabolic differences, and lack evidence of the canonical stress response (Gasch et al., 2016; Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Naturally aneuploid yeast show no detectable metabolic differences compared to laboratory strain W303.
source: In contrast to well-studied laboratory strain W303, naturally aneuploid yeast show only subtle growth defects, no detectable metabolic differences, and lack evidence of the canonical stress response (Gasch et al., 2016; Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Naturally aneuploid yeast lack evidence of the canonical stress response.
source: In contrast to well-studied laboratory strain W303, naturally aneuploid yeast show only subtle growth defects, no detectable metabolic differences, and lack evidence of the canonical stress response (Gasch et al., 2016; Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The relative tolerance of wild yeast to aneuploidy is not a result of adaptation.
source: The relative tolerance is not a result of adaptation: we showed that naturally euploid strains selected for chromosome amplification also showed relatively mild growth defects, and euploid derivatives of aneuploid isolates grew similarly to the aneuploid parent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from previous work by the authors.

claim: Chromosome amplification in some wild yeast strains is generally stable.
source: Although some strains show variable karyotypes over time, picking up or losing chromosomes during division, chromosome amplification in other strains is generally stable (Gasch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Many wild yeast strains tolerate chromosome amplification whereas W303 cannot.
source: Thus, many wild yeast strains tolerate chromosome amplification whereas W303 cannot.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in previous work by the authors.

claim: W303 carries a premature stop codon in SSD1 that deletes 44% of the Ssd1 protein including conserved RNA binding domains.
source: This locus harbors a premature stop codon in W303 that deletes 44% of the Ssd1 protein including conserved RNA binding domains (Uesono et al., 1997; Sutton et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ssd1 is best characterized for regulating localization and translation of cell-wall destined mRNAs.
source: Ssd1 is best characterized for regulating localization and translation of cell-wall destined mRNAs, delivered by Ssd1 to the growing bud during active growth but to P-bodies for translational silencing following stress or mitotic defects (Jansen et al., 2009; Kurischko et al., 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ssd1 delivers cell-wall destined mRNAs to the growing bud during active growth but to P-bodies for translational silencing following stress or mitotic defects.

claim: Ssd1 has a role in aging and quiescence.
source: Ssd1 has also been implicated in a large number of suppressor screens and has a role in aging and quiescence (Miles et al., 2019; Li et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2018).

claim: The W303 premature stop codon in SSD1 underlies several phenotypic differences reported between W303 and other strains.
source: W303 carries a premature stop codon that ablates RNA binding domains, which underlies several phenotypic differences reported between W303 and other strains (Kaeberlein et al., 2004; Moriya and Isono, 1999; Ohyama et al., 2010; Uesono et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SSD1 deletion had little effect on the growth of euploid YPS1009.
source: SSD1 deletion had little effect on the growth of euploid YPS1009 but significantly retarded YPS1009_Chr12 proliferation, comparable to W303_Chr12 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SSD1 deletion significantly retarded YPS1009_Chr12 proliferation, comparable to W303_Chr12.
source: SSD1 deletion had little effect on the growth of euploid YPS1009 but significantly retarded YPS1009_Chr12 proliferation, comparable to W303_Chr12 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Growth rate was restored if YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ cells lost the extra chromosome during passaging.
source: Growth rate was restored if cells lost the extra chromosome during passaging (Figure 1D, star) or if SSD1YPS1009 was reintroduced (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Growth rate was restored if SSD1YPS1009 was reintroduced into YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ cells.
source: Growth rate was restored if cells lost the extra chromosome during passaging (Figure 1D, star) or if SSD1YPS1009 was reintroduced (Figure 1E).

claim: SSD1 deletion sensitized NCYC110_Chr8 cells to chromosome amplification.
source: To test if Ssd1's role was exclusive to this genetic background or chromosome amplification, we deleted SSD1 in naturally aneuploid, diploid West African strain tetrasomic for Chr 8 (NCYC110_Chr8) and in a derived aneuploid vineyard strain, KCY40_Chr8 (Hose et al., 2015). SSD1 deletion sensitized cells to chromosome amplification, showing that the effect is independent of genetic background and duplicated chromosome (and is thus also independent of the rDNA locus on Chr 12) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SSD1 deletion sensitized KCY40_Chr8 cells to chromosome amplification.
source: To test if Ssd1's role was exclusive to this genetic background or chromosome amplification, we deleted SSD1 in naturally aneuploid, diploid West African strain tetrasomic for Chr 8 (NCYC110_Chr8) and in a derived aneuploid vineyard strain, KCY40_Chr8 (Hose et al., 2015). SSD1 deletion sensitized cells to chromosome amplification, showing that the effect is independent of genetic background and duplicated chromosome (and is thus also independent of the rDNA locus on Chr 12) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The effect of SSD1 on aneuploidy tolerance is independent of genetic background and duplicated chromosome.
source: SSD1 deletion sensitized cells to chromosome amplification, showing that the effect is independent of genetic background and duplicated chromosome (and is thus also independent of the rDNA locus on Chr 12) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that SSD1 deletion affects multiple strain backgrounds and chromosome amplifications.

claim: Reintroducing the YPS1009 allele of SSD1 complemented the aneuploidy sensitivity of multiple strain backgrounds.
source: Reintroducing the YPS1009 allele of SSD1 complemented the aneuploidy sensitivity of multiple strain backgrounds (Figure 1E), whereas the W303 allele provided no complementation in the NCYC110_Chr8 ssd1Δ strain and partial complementation in YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The W303 allele of SSD1 provided no complementation in the NCYC110_Chr8 ssd1Δ strain.
source: Reintroducing the YPS1009 allele of SSD1 complemented the aneuploidy sensitivity of multiple strain backgrounds (Figure 1E), whereas the W303 allele provided no complementation in the NCYC110_Chr8 ssd1Δ strain and partial complementation in YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The W303 allele of SSD1 provided partial complementation in YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ.

evidence: This claim is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expressing the YPS1009 allele of SSD1 in W303_Chr12 largely corrected its sensitivity.
source: Importantly, expressing the YPS1009 allele in W303_Chr12 largely corrected its sensitivity (with a remaining contribution likely from the adenine auxotrophy, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), demonstrating that the ssd1W303 allele is responsible for aneuploidy sensitivity in W303.
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation data shown in Figure 1E and related supplementary figures.

claim: The ssd1W303 allele is responsible for aneuploidy sensitivity in W303.
source: Importantly, expressing the YPS1009 allele in W303_Chr12 largely corrected its sensitivity (with a remaining contribution likely from the adenine auxotrophy, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), demonstrating that the ssd1W303 allele is responsible for aneuploidy sensitivity in W303.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the complementation experiment showing that the YPS1009 allele rescues W303 sensitivity.

claim: Ssd1 plays a generalizable role in tolerating chromosome amplification across multiple strains and chromosome duplications.
source: Thus, Ssd1 plays a generalizable role in tolerating chromosome amplification across multiple strains and chromosome duplications.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that SSD1 affects aneuploidy tolerance in multiple genetic backgrounds and chromosome amplifications.

claim: W303 studies reported a transcriptomic signature of aneuploidy independent of amplified chromosome identity.
source: W303 studies reported a transcriptomic signature of aneuploidy independent of amplified chromosome identity, but this is not seen in wild aneuploid strains (Torres et al., 2007; Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The transcriptomic signature of aneuploidy seen in W303 is not seen in wild aneuploid strains.
source: W303 studies reported a transcriptomic signature of aneuploidy independent of amplified chromosome identity, but this is not seen in wild aneuploid strains (Torres et al., 2007; Hose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: 861 genes showed altered expression in both YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ and NCYC110_Chr8 ssd1Δ mutants compared to their isogenic wild-type aneuploids.
source: We identified 861 genes with altered expression in both YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ and NCYC110_Chr8 ssd1Δ mutants compared to their isogenic wild-type aneuploids (false discovery rate, FDR < 0.05, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Induced genes in ssd1Δ aneuploids showed little change in euploid YPS1009 ssd1Δ but were up-regulated when SSD1 was deleted in the context of Chr12 amplification.
source: Induced genes showed little change in euploid YPS1009 ssd1Δ but were up-regulated when SSD1 was deleted in the context of Chr12 amplification.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NCYC110 showed a weak expression signature in euploid ssd1Δ cells that was exacerbated when Chr8 was amplified.
source: NCYC110 showed similar trends, except that in this strain we observed a weak expression signature in euploid ssd1Δ cells that was exacerbated when Chr8 was amplified.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The transcriptome response in ssd1Δ aneuploids effectively recapitulates the expression signature seen in W303 aneuploids.

evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data to previous literature, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The transcriptome response in ssd1Δ aneuploids was exacerbated with increasing DNA content in W303 carrying multiple extra chromosomes.
source: The response was exacerbated with increasing DNA content in W303 carrying multiple extra chromosomes (Figure 2A).

claim: The previously reported aneuploidy transcriptome signature results from defective Ssd1 function, independent of affected chromosome, exacerbated with additional DNA content.

evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing that ssd1Δ recapitulates the W303 aneuploidy signature.

claim: Significantly more YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ cells accumulated VHL-GFP foci compared to wild type.
source: We found that significantly more YPS1009_Chr12 ssd1Δ cells accumulated VHL-GFP foci compared to wild type (Figure 2B).

claim: Wild-type aneuploids showed no obvious difference in the number of Hsp104-GFP foci compared to euploids.
source: Wild-type aneuploids showed no obvious difference in the number of Hsp104-GFP foci compared to euploids (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that gross protein aggregation is not a universal feature of aneuploid yeast.

claim: Gross protein aggregation is not a universal feature of aneuploid yeast.

claim: Mutant aneuploids lacking SSD1 showed a higher proportion of cells with Hsp104-GFP foci, and more foci within those cells, compared to wild-type aneuploids.

claim: Ssd1 was previously implicated in protein homeostasis after heat shock.
source: Ssd1 was previously implicated in protein homeostasis after heat shock (Mir et al., 2009), but our results demonstrate that chromosome amplification in the absence of other stresses is enough to provoke misfolding in ssd1Δ cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Chromosome amplification in the absence of other stresses is enough to provoke misfolding in ssd1Δ cells.

evidence: This claim is supported by VHL-GFP and Hsp104-GFP data showing protein misfolding in ssd1Δ aneuploids.

claim: Myriad signatures of W303 aneuploidy can occur due to defective Ssd1.
